The biggest story this AM is oil and bond yields rising at the same time. Brent is at 105.11 (+2.03, +1.97%) and WTI at 93.70 (+1.54). Japan's 10Y yield jumped 9.1bp to 3.08, while US stock futures extend yesterday's selloff. At the prior close the S&P 500 fell -0.75% to 7706.03, the Nasdaq Composite -1.13% to 26936.04, the Dow -0.68% to 51511.59 and the Russell 2000 -1.77% to 2838.66. VIX rose to 15.96 from 15.18. Pre-market, ES is 7731.5 (-41.0, -0.53%), NQ 30465.75 (-0.97%) and Dow futures 51720.0 (-0.29%). US Treasuries are rallying at the front end: the 2Y is 4.8433 (-5.4bp) and the 10Y 5.0935 (-2.07bp), with the 30Y flat at 5.40. That steepening is consistent with growth worries after last week's Fed hike rather than inflation relief. Europe is slightly softer (Euro Stoxx 50 -0.19%, STOXX 600 -0.21%), the FTSE is flat to up (+0.08%) on its energy weighting, and the Nikkei closed +0.76% at 65513.99. Sentiment is cautious rather than panicked. Credit spreads remain near historic tights (IG 0.76, HY 2.74), which says the selloff so far is about positioning and rates, not credit.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

A move to about 1.00 would require a sustained equity drawdown of roughly 10% plus a second Fed hike. The 2000-era reference of 1.22 would require a growth scare or a credit event. For HY, 2.33 (the historic min) is the downside limit; 3.25–3.50 is the first stress zone if oil stays above 100 and small caps keep underperforming. Above 4.00 would signal a genuine default-cycle repricing. With yields at 5%+ and spreads this tight, the carry cushion against a spread shock is thin.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.98 vol points (81th percentile of the 26 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 95.5 (69th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 98bp (steeper by 35bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 73% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (106bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.11 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 73%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed dashboard says this cycle's froth is concentrated in semiconductors and credit, not spread across the whole equity market. Semis at 93% of the 2000 valuation marker make Micron's Sept 30 report a key test for the AI trade. Credit tightness beyond 2000 levels means a spread shock would hit from a starting point of zero cushion. What argues against an imminent 2000-style top: retail sentiment is bearish (AAII bull-bear -15.4), consumer confidence is subdued (89.4), and margin-debt growth (33.7% YoY) is less than half its 2000 pace. What argues for caution: CAPE at 41.29 is the second-highest reading on record, the top-10 weight is about 35% (analyst estimate from web sources), and the Fed has just started hiking into a 5% 10Y. The 2000 top also came roughly a year into a Fed tightening cycle. Analyst view: late-stage, not terminal. The Warsh hiking path is the catalyst to watch.

⚔️Iran War

The US-Israel war on Iran began February 28, 2026 (Wikipedia/Britannica) and is now in a mixed phase of diplomacy and pressure. On September 23, Al Jazeera's live blog reported that Tehran said it was ready for 'dialogue, diplomacy without force' and that President Trump confirmed a 'very good meeting' with Iran at the UN. Days earlier, on September 20, Tehran warned of a 'painful' response to any new US attacks and called for an end to the war and the lifting of the US naval blockade. The blockade is the key oil-supply channel. Regionally, reports in this cycle's search note the Saudi-led coalition intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu. Yanbu is a Red Sea oil export hub, which helps explain today's +1.97% move in Brent to 105.11. The Iranian and Ukrainian foreign ministers also met at the UNGA, their first meeting since a July incident in the Caspian Sea. Market read (analyst): diplomacy caps the tail risk, but as long as the blockade holds and energy infrastructure is targeted, oil carries a risk premium.

Sources: Iran war updates: Tehran ready for 'dialogue, diplomacy without force' — Al Jazeera (Sep 23, 2026) · Iran war updates: Tehran warns of 'painful' response if US launches attacks — Al Jazeera (Sep 20, 2026) · 2026 Iran war — Wikipedia · 2026 Iran war — Britannica · JINSA Iran War Update: September 1–2, 2026

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting: a lean toward another 25bp hike (analyst estimate ~55%) versus a hold (~45%). On September 16 the FOMC hiked unanimously by 25bp to 3.75%–4.00%, its first hike since 2023. Warsh framed it as 'removing the dose of accommodation' and has said the Fed may have 'work to do'. The US 2Y at 4.8433, well above the 4.00% upper bound, suggests markets already price further tightening (inference). Oil above 100 makes a pause harder to justify.

~1 YEAR

Analyst estimate: fed funds at 4.25%–4.75% in a year, with the hiking cycle ending once core PCE (3.34415) turns clearly toward 2%. Inference from his prior writings (not confirmed in this run's sources): he may prefer shrinking the balance sheet to rate cuts once inflation turns, and a 'quieter' Fed with less forward guidance. That means more meeting-to-meeting volatility in rates.

At Jackson Hole (Aug 28, 2026) Warsh said he was 'committed to a discipline, not to a decision'. He called the 2% PCE target 'a firm, fixed target' and advocated a 'quieter' central bank (Fed speech; CNBC; Washington Post). At the September 16 press conference he framed the hike as proof the economy is strong enough to handle it, and argued that stable prices help the least well-off most (CNN; Fed transcript). Inference: this is a rules-minded, inflation-first chair. With core PCE at 3.34415 and Brent above 100, the bar to stop hiking is high. The bar to cut is very high absent a credit event, and credit spreads (IG 0.76) show none.

Sources: Keynote remarks by Chairman Warsh at the 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium — Federal Reserve · September 16, 2026 Chairman Warsh's Press Conference (preliminary transcript) — Federal Reserve · What Kevin Warsh said about the Fed's first rate hike since 2023 — CNN · Fed meeting recap: Warsh says inflation is still too high as Fed hikes — CNBC · Fed Chairman Warsh expresses concern about inflation, advocates for 'quieter' central bank — CNBC · Fed chair Warsh, concerned about inflation, says bank may have 'work to do' — Washington Post
